doc.title: Charles Calello interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 21, 2025

title: Making A Lover's Concerto
summary: Calello explains the song's origins with Linzer and Randell, the Stop in the Name of Love intro, and the one-take fourth song of the session.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: You can’t see this but I’m looking at the wall in front of me and I have a printout of the top 100 Charlie Calello hits and arrangements. And I’ve zoomed in on a couple. And I want to sort of dissect the “Lover’s Concerto” if you don’t mind. Because as you said, this hit a nerve with me. And I noticed that, I really got into the deep end with this because I was timing, how long was the melody. And you know the first phrase is like 16 seconds, and then there’s two of them. A 16 second intro and then the whole first verse I’ll call it, is 46 seconds. So part of an arrangement is like well we need more than a minute of music here. So we have to stretch this out. And was it your idea to go through five keys?

No. In fact when I made that record – I’ll back up a couple of beats – Sandy Linzer wrote the song with Denny Randell. Sandy Linzer also wrote “Dawn (Go Away)” with Bob Gaudio, and he became one of the writers of the Four Seasons. My father actually introduced me to him. So after they had a couple of hit records with Bob Crewe they

decided to produce a record on their own. So I would sit with them and they would play me the song and then I would write the arrangements while they were sitting there. And what was interesting about it was we worked on the arrangements together. But now I did something that I didn’t realize I did. On the introduction where it started with the concerto [scats] – right after that I wrote the intro to “Stop In The Name of Love.” What was it – and unconsciously I wrote it because it went like this [scats]. And when I heard it on the radio I said to myself how could you do that. But the funny part about it – the funny part about it – it just needed something there and it seemed to fit the groove. And we never got busted for it, nobody ever called it to my attention. And as I would remind people about it they’d say, “Oh yeah it really does that.” But now when they played me the song they played me the modulations. My father actually played trumpet on that record. But this was really funny, it was the fourth song on the session, to give you some idea of how quickly we made the record. Vinnie Bell, who was one of the guitar players on the session said, “Charlie, you’ve got five minutes. Are you going to get this fourth song done?” So I said, I said, “Yeah, let’s do it right now.” So I played the intro, only the intro and first verse, just to get the feel. And I said to the engineer, “Record it.” It was the first take. There was only one take on the track. So when we finished the record, you know we didn’t have the singers on yet, but the pop song that we were looking to release we finished it. It still sounded great but it was never released and eventually it was a hit by another group, a group from Australia, I forget the name of the song. But “A Lover’s Concerto” was like the fourth song on the date. It wasn’t something that we intended to even release as a single.
